reference.source: Oxford Textbook of Old Age Psychiatry
clinicalPearls: Syndrome of extreme self-neglect, domestic squalor, social withdrawal, and often hoarding (syllogomania), with a characteristic lack of shame or insight.
Typically affects older adults living alone and may occur with or without a diagnosable mental illness.
The eponym, drawn from the Greek philosopher Diogenes, is widely regarded as a misnomer.
Around half of cases have no primary psychiatric diagnosis; the remainder are associated with frontal-lobe dysfunction, dementia, alcohol misuse, or psychosis.
Frontal and executive dysfunction is a recurrent theme, with behaviour reflecting impaired judgement and self-regulation.
Frequently comes to attention through neighbours, environmental health, or crisis rather than self-referral.
Carries high morbidity and mortality, with presentations including malnutrition, hypothermia, infestation, or untreated medical illness.
Capacity assessment and multi-agency working with social care and environmental health are central to management.
reference.pathophysiology: Diogenes syndrome is a behavioural syndrome rather than a single disease, characterised by breakdown of self-care and of socially normative standards of cleanliness. A substantial proportion of cases are linked to frontal-lobe and executive dysfunction, whether from neurodegeneration, cerebrovascular disease, or alcohol-related damage, impairing planning, judgement, and insight. Premorbid personality traits such as aloofness, stubbornness, and suspiciousness, together with adverse life events, may precipitate decompensation in vulnerable older people. In others the picture is secondary to dementia, psychosis, depression, or obsessive hoarding, and the final common presentation is profound self-neglect with abnormal decision-making about the home environment.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic psychotic illness such as schizophrenia
Learning disability or longstanding personality difficulties
additionalInvestigations: Cognitive assessment and neuropsychological or executive-function testing
Neuroimaging (MRI or CT) for frontal and cerebrovascular pathology
Capacity assessment regarding care and residence
Nutritional and physical health screen (full blood count, metabolic panel, vitamins, thyroid function)
Home and environmental assessment via occupational therapy and environmental health
redFlags: Untreated serious physical illness or pressure injuries
Fire or public-health hazard arising from hoarding
Loss of capacity with inability to keep oneself safe
reference.prognosis: Mortality is high, particularly where physical complications are advanced, and recurrence of squalor after intervention is common; outcome improves with treatment of any underlying disorder and sustained multi-agency support.
pitfalls: Assuming that self-neglect equates to lack of capacity, or the reverse, without formal assessment
Attributing the picture solely to eccentricity and missing dementia or depression
One-off clearance of the home without addressing the underlying cause, leading to relapse
references: Oxford Textbook of Old Age Psychiatry
